title: Strategic Compensation, Labor Relations, and HR Law
objective: Evaluate compensation strategies, interpret key employment laws, and apply HR practices that balance organizational goals with employee rights.
body:
**Compensation** is one of the most powerful levers an organization controls. Total compensation includes **direct pay** (base salary, bonuses, commissions) and **indirect pay** — the full package of benefits such as health insurance, retirement plans, paid time off, and employee assistance programs. Designing compensation well requires balancing internal equity, external competitiveness, and individual performance.

**Internal equity** means employees perceive pay as fair relative to colleagues in similar roles — typically ensured through **job evaluation** methods that rank positions by their relative value. **External equity** means pay is competitive with the labor market, determined through **compensation surveys** that benchmark salaries against industry peers. Organizations that pay below market risk losing talent to competitors; those that consistently overpay may sacrifice profitability. Most organizations set a **pay range** with a minimum, midpoint, and maximum for each job grade to balance both concerns.

Compensation philosophy comes in two broad forms. A **market leader strategy** pays above median to attract and retain top talent — common in high-tech industries where talent is scarce. A **market follower strategy** (also called market matching) pays at or near the median, while a lag strategy pays below it, often compensating with strong non-monetary benefits or growth opportunities. **Pay-for-performance** systems tie compensation increases to individual or team results, including merit pay, profit-sharing, and **gainsharing** (where teams share in the financial gains from their productivity improvements).

Effective HR practice requires fluency in key employment laws. The **Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA)** establishes the federal minimum wage, mandates overtime pay (1.5× the regular rate) for non-exempt employees working more than 40 hours per week, and distinguishes between exempt and non-exempt classifications. Title VII of the **Civil Rights Act of 1964** prohibits employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin. The **Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA)** requires employers to provide **reasonable accommodations** to qualified individuals with disabilities, unless doing so creates an **undue hardship** for the organization. The **Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA)** entitles eligible employees to up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave for qualifying family or medical reasons.

**Labor relations** governs the relationship between employers and unions. The **National Labor Relations Act (NLRA)** protects employees' rights to organize, bargain collectively, and engage in concerted activity. When employees unionize, management and union representatives negotiate a **collective bargaining agreement (CBA)** covering wages, hours, and working conditions. HR professionals must understand **unfair labor practices** — illegal actions by employers (such as retaliating against organizing employees) or unions — to avoid costly violations.

The strategic HR professional recognizes that compensation, legal compliance, and labor relations are not isolated activities. A compensation system that inadvertently creates pay disparities along protected-class lines creates legal liability. A disciplinary process that is not consistently applied can become an unfair labor practice. Integrating these areas is the mark of mature HR strategy.
examples: A software company benchmarks its engineer salaries annually using a published compensation survey and sets its pay ranges at the 75th percentile of the market — a deliberate market leader strategy to reduce turnover in a competitive talent market.

An employee with a mobility impairment requests a standing desk and a closer parking space; the employer provides both at modest cost, satisfying the ADA's reasonable accommodation requirement without incurring undue hardship.

A warehouse operation introduces a gainsharing plan that pays each crew a quarterly bonus when throughput exceeds the baseline by 10%, directly linking team productivity gains to shared financial rewards.

questions.stem: An employer pays female engineers 15% less than male engineers in identical roles with equivalent experience. This most directly violates:
choices: The Family and Medical Leave Act
Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
The National Labor Relations Act
The Americans with Disabilities Act
questions.explanation: Title VII prohibits sex-based employment discrimination, which includes compensation disparities for the same work. The FMLA governs leave rights and is not applicable here.

questions.stem: Under the FLSA, a non-exempt employee works 46 hours in one week at a base rate of $20/hour. What is the correct total pay for that week?
questions.explanation: The employee earns $20 × 40 = $800 for regular hours, plus 6 overtime hours at $30 each ($20 × 1.5) = $180, for a total of $980. Paying the flat rate of $920 for all 46 hours would violate FLSA's overtime provision.

questions.stem: A company conducts a salary survey and adjusts pay to match the median for each role. This compensation approach is called:
choices: Market leader strategy
Pay compression
Market follower strategy
Gainsharing
questions.explanation: Paying at the market median is a market follower strategy, which meets but does not exceed competitive rates. A market leader strategy deliberately pays above the median to gain a talent acquisition advantage.

questions.stem: An employee with severe anxiety disorder requests permission to work from home two days per week. Under the ADA, the employer must:
choices: Automatically approve the request regardless of business impact
Engage in an interactive process to assess whether the accommodation is reasonable
Deny the request because mental health conditions are not covered
Transfer the employee to a different department
questions.explanation: The ADA requires an interactive dialogue between employer and employee to explore reasonable accommodations; automatic approval is not the standard. Mental health conditions are covered under the ADA when they substantially limit a major life activity.

questions.stem: A manufacturing plant's HR director discovers that supervisors have been firing employees who attended a union organizing meeting. This is most likely an:
choices: Acceptable management prerogative under employment-at-will
Unfair labor practice under the NLRA
Violation of the FLSA overtime rules
Reasonable business decision protected by the First Amendment
questions.explanation: The NLRA protects employees' rights to organize and engage in concerted activity; retaliating against employees for union activity is a classic unfair labor practice. Employment-at-will does not override NLRA protections.

questions.stem: The purpose of a pay range with a minimum, midpoint, and maximum for each job grade is PRIMARILY to:
choices: Eliminate bonuses and commissions from the compensation structure
Balance internal equity with external market competitiveness within each role
Ensure all employees earn the same salary regardless of experience
Comply with FLSA minimum wage requirements
questions.explanation: Pay ranges allow organizations to reward varying levels of experience and performance within a role while keeping pay anchored to market benchmarks, balancing internal equity (fairness among peers) with external equity (market competitiveness).

questions.stem: A hospital implements a plan where nursing units receive a share of cost savings they generate through reduced supply waste. This is an example of:
choices: Merit pay
Profit-sharing
Gainsharing
Commission-based pay
questions.explanation: Gainsharing distributes a portion of the financial gains from team productivity or cost improvements back to the contributing employees. Profit-sharing distributes a portion of overall company profits rather than unit-level performance gains.

questions.stem: Under the FMLA, an eligible employee may take up to 12 weeks of leave that is:
choices: Paid and job-protected
Unpaid and job-protected
Paid but not job-protected
Unpaid and at the employer's discretion to restore the position
questions.explanation: FMLA provides up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave, meaning the employer must restore the employee to the same or equivalent position upon return. The law does not require paid leave, though some employers offer it voluntarily.

flashcards.definition: The perception that pay is fair relative to colleagues holding similar roles within the same organization, typically ensured through systematic job evaluation.
A federal law that establishes the minimum wage, requires overtime pay at 1.5 times the regular rate for non-exempt employees working more than 40 hours per week, and regulates child labor.

Under the ADA, a modification to a job, work environment, or the way work is performed that enables a qualified individual with a disability to perform essential job functions without causing undue hardship to the employer.
A legally binding contract negotiated between management and a union that defines wages, hours, benefits, and working conditions for covered employees.
A pay-for-performance plan in which employees share in the financial savings or productivity gains their work group generates, linking team behavior directly to compensation.
